note: Text is as checked (served text, including the round-4 rationales for Q1.6 and Q6.0). Excludes the 40 round-1 ids (ROUND1_IDS) and the 120 ids in spot-check-round2-sample.json and spot-check-round3-sample.json. No item text was changed by this round. This file is the record of what was checked.

items.text: Adding a production DNS record after 1500 against shop policy is:
options: A change
A repair
An incident
Optional documentation
items.correct: A change
items.explanation: Adding a production DNS record introduces something new on shared infrastructure, so it is a change and goes through the shop’s change process, which here forbids it after 1500. A repair only restores a known-good state (reseat RAM, replace a failed disk), nothing has broken yet so it is not an incident, and documentation is never optional for work that can affect other people. See 1.3. Source: ITIL 4 Change enablement practice guide (a change is any addition, modification or removal that could affect services); course 1.3.

items.text: While handling RAM modules, which practice reduces ESD risk most directly?
options: Holding modules by the gold contacts
Storing modules in a plastic bag
A grounded wrist strap and an ESD-safe mat
Rubber-soled shoes
items.correct: A grounded wrist strap and an ESD-safe mat
items.explanation: A grounded wrist strap and ESD mat keep you and the component at the same potential.

items.text: Which note can the next watch actually use?
options: VPN is broken again, user says it worked last week and wants it fixed fast
User cannot connect, tried rebooting, please look into it when you have time
Hotel Wi-Fi is bad, so I told the user to find a better network and to call us back later today
VPN client 4.2.1, error 809, LAN ping OK, gateway ping fails, since the weekend update
items.correct: VPN client 4.2.1, error 809, LAN ping OK, gateway ping fails, since the weekend update
items.explanation: This note records the version, the error code and two tests with their results (LAN ping works, gateway ping fails), plus when it started, so the next technician can pick up at the gateway. “VPN is broken again” and the other notes give only opinions and requests, with no test a peer can build on. See 1.3.

items.text: A caller says they are the CFO and need their password reset now. What do you do first?
options: Verify identity using the approved method
Reset it and read it out on the call
Email the new password to any address given
Disable MFA so they can sign in
items.correct: Verify identity using the approved method
items.explanation: Identity verification comes before any credential change; urgency is a common social-engineering pressure.

items.text: M.2 stick in the short slot on the card. Storage word?
options: storage hdd
storage usb
storage nvme
storage sata
items.correct: storage nvme
items.explanation: On the hw-board bench card, the stick in the short M.2 slot is the NVMe drive, so the interface word is nvme (a 2.5-inch drive in the SATA tray would be sata). “storage sata” is the tempting wrong answer because some M.2 sticks are SATA drives; the word names the interface the course card documents, not the slot shape or the brand. See 2.5.

items.text: You install an M.2 NVMe SSD but the OS installer only lists a SATA HDD. BIOS shows the NVMe under a PCIe slot. What should you check first?
options: The drive is larger than MBR allows
The SATA HDD must be removed first
The UEFI storage mode (RAID/VMD) needs a driver
Secure Boot blocks NVMe drives in Setup
items.correct: The UEFI storage mode (RAID/VMD) needs a driver
items.explanation: Firmware already sees the drive, so it is healthy; the installer cannot see it because the controller is in a RAID/VMD mode that needs a driver (or the slot shares lanes with SATA). Change the storage mode or load the driver.

items.text: Long beeps + MEM, no video. Display cable first?
options: Only if the monitor is new
No. That is POST memory
Yes
Yes, if it uses HDMI
items.correct: No. That is POST memory
items.explanation: Long beeps with a memory code and no video is a POST memory failure: the board stops before it ever sends a picture, so the display cable is not the next check. “Yes, if it uses HDMI” mixes the display order into a POST fault; reseat and test the memory first. See 2.5 / 3.4.

items.text: Why list disk before imaging?
options: To convert to MBR every time
To skip About
To know which handle is the OS disk
To clean every disk automatically
items.correct: To know which handle is the OS disk
items.explanation: Disk numbers such as Disk 0 are handles that can change between machines and boots, so list disk shows which handle is the OS disk before anything is imaged or written. Cleaning or converting disks “automatically” is the failure this step prevents: run against the wrong handle, it destroys the wrong disk. See 2.6.

items.text: M.2 is the slot. NVMe is:
options: A protocol that often uses that slot
Always the same thing as M.2
A PSU rating
A board form factor, the same as ATX
items.correct: A protocol that often uses that slot
items.explanation: M.2 is a physical slot and card shape; NVMe is the protocol a drive uses over PCIe, and it often uses an M.2 slot. Calling them “always the same thing” is the classic mix-up: an M.2 card can be a SATA drive, which an NVMe-only slot will not accept. See 3.1.

items.text: RAID 0 if one disk dies:
options: Firmware fixes it
The volume is gone
The volume stays up
Parity rebuilds overnight
items.correct: The volume is gone
items.explanation: RAID 0 stripes data across the disks with no parity or mirror, so losing one disk loses the whole volume. “Parity rebuilds overnight” describes RAID 5 or 6; RAID 0 has nothing to rebuild from, which is why it is never used for data you cannot lose. See 3.2.

items.text: Unstable workstation capstone: you change four parts at once. Problem?
options: It takes too long
Nothing, if the PC works afterwards
It voids the warranty
You cannot tell what fixed it
items.correct: You cannot tell what fixed it
items.explanation: Changing four parts at once means you cannot tell which change fixed the fault, so the note cannot explain it and the next technician cannot learn from it. “Nothing, if the PC works afterwards” ignores that: change one thing, test, write the result, then decide on the next change. See 3.5.

items.text: POST already OK, panel is dark. First idea?
options: clean disk
Disable Secure Boot
Cable and input on the panel
Replace the motherboard first
items.correct: Cable and input on the panel
items.explanation: POST already passes, so the PC itself starts; a dark panel then points to the display path: the cable and the monitor’s input selection. Replacing the motherboard skips the cheap display-path checks and replaces a part that has already shown it works. See 3.4.

items.text: Which command shows a laptop battery’s design capacity and full charge capacity?
options: ipconfig /batteryinfo /all
chkdsk C: /battery
msinfo32 /report power
powercfg /batteryreport
items.correct: powercfg /batteryreport
items.explanation: powercfg /batteryreport writes an HTML report with both capacities and their history.

items.text: Mail syncs on cellular but not on the office Wi-Fi. What should you check next?
options: The phone’s eSIM carrier profile
The battery report on the phone
The Activation Lock status
Which SSID and address it has
items.correct: Which SSID and address it has
items.explanation: The device and account work; the building Wi-Fi path (wrong SSID, guest network, proxy) is the suspect.

items.text: One user cannot print from the browser; Word on the same PC works. Where do you start?
options: Replace the floor printer
Rebuild the print server for the floor
Swap the PSU
App / driver path for that browser
items.correct: App / driver path for that browser
items.explanation: Word prints from the same PC, so the printer, network and print server all work; only the browser’s print path (its print settings or the driver it uses) differs. Rebuilding the print server treats one application on one PC as a floor-wide outage. See 4.3.

items.text: A dual-stack host reaches IPv4 sites but not IPv6-only services. ipconfig shows a link-local IPv6 only. What is missing?
options: A second IPv4 default gateway
Disabling IPv4 so IPv6 is preferred
Router advertisements or DHCPv6 address
An IPv6 DNS server set on the client
items.correct: Router advertisements or DHCPv6 address
items.explanation: A link-local (fe80::) address alone means no router advertisement or DHCPv6 provided a global address.

items.text: Outlook loops but ping to the mail server IP works. NIC is dead?
options: No. The path is up; check name, account, service
Yes. Outlook failing means the NIC failed
Yes, if the address it shows is in the APIPA range
Yes, if the link light is blinking
items.correct: No. The path is up; check name, account, service
items.explanation: A successful ping to the mail server’s IP proves the NIC, link and route work, so the problem is higher up: the name, the account or the mail service. “Outlook failing means the NIC failed” ignores that evidence; a dead NIC could not ping anything. See 5.2.

items.text: A PC has a valid lease but cannot ping its default gateway. Which layer is next to check?
options: The local LAN and the gateway
The DNS server and its records
The web proxy configuration
The application’s service port
items.correct: The local LAN and the gateway
items.explanation: Stop at the first failing step: the gateway is unreachable, so name and service tests would prove nothing yet.

items.text: A SOHO router was set to a static WAN IP but the ISP only provides DHCP. Symptom: WAN LED up, no Internet. Fix?
options: Point the router at a public DNS resolver
Enable NAT on the LAN interface instead
Set the WAN interface to obtain an address automatically
Disable the DHCP server on the LAN side
items.correct: Set the WAN interface to obtain an address automatically
items.explanation: The ISP assigns the WAN address by DHCP, so a static WAN setting leaves the router with no valid upstream address.

items.text: A VM is:
options: A remote desktop session
A guest PC made of files, running on a host
A physical server rack-mounted in a data centre
A backup copy of a hard drive
items.correct: A guest PC made of files, running on a host
items.explanation: A virtual machine is a guest computer made of files (virtual disks and configuration) that runs on a host’s hypervisor, so the Windows on this bench may itself be a guest. A remote desktop session is only a remote view of some computer, physical or virtual. A rack server is physical hardware that may host VMs, and a backup copy of a disk does not run. See 6.1. Source: NIST SP 800-125, Guide to Security for Full Virtualization Technologies (host, hypervisor, guest OS).

items.text: Whole tenant cannot open mail; ipconfig on the laptop is fine. Next?
options: format C:
Open the PSU
Vendor / tenant path, not a local disk
Reimage the first laptop that reported it
items.correct: Vendor / tenant path, not a local disk
items.explanation: The laptop’s IP configuration is fine and every user in the tenant has the same failure, so the common factor is the SaaS tenant or the vendor: go to the vendor or tenant status path. Reimaging the first laptop treats a shared service outage as one device’s fault and destroys evidence. See 6.2.

items.text: After cloning a VM, both clones fight for the same IP and computer name on the LAN. What was omitted?
options: Disable DHCP on the lab LAN
Add a second virtual NIC to each clone
Take a snapshot of each clone
Generalise (Sysprep) for unique identity
items.correct: Generalise (Sysprep) for unique identity
items.explanation: Clones need a generalised image (Sysprep) or regenerated identity, plus unique names and addresses.

items.text: Capstone miss: diskpart on a mail-SaaS outage. Why fail?
options: You followed 7.2
SaaS requires clean
You forgot to run list disk
You crossed fault domains
items.correct: You crossed fault domains
items.explanation: Running diskpart on a PC during a mail-SaaS outage works on the local disk when the fault is in the vendor’s service: it crosses fault domains, and it risks data while testing nothing relevant. “Always list disk” is a good habit for disk work, but it does not make disk work the right domain here. See 7.4.

items.text: A help desk agent escalates without listing steps already tried. What professionalism issue does this create?
options: It breaches change control
It shortens time to repair
Tier 2 repeats work and lacks context
Nothing — tier 2 retests anyway
items.correct: Tier 2 repeats work and lacks context
items.explanation: Without the steps already tried, tier 2 repeats work and lacks context, so resolution slows.

items.text: During a high-impact outage, what should users hear while the owning team works?
options: Nothing until the fix has been confirmed by the owning team
Status updates at an agreed interval, even if no change
A guess at the root cause to keep them calm
Instructions to restart their PCs every hour
items.correct: Status updates at an agreed interval, even if no change
items.explanation: Regular, honest updates manage expectations; guesses and silence both erode trust.

items.text: Clean install versus in-place:
options: Neither one counts as a change
Clean wipes the OS volume; in-place tries to keep apps and files
Clean keeps apps and files; in-place wipes the whole OS volume
They are the same process with different names
items.correct: Clean wipes the OS volume; in-place tries to keep apps and files
items.explanation: A clean install wipes the OS volume and starts again. An in-place upgrade or repair reinstalls Windows while trying to keep apps, files and settings. Both are changes that need a ticket, and they are not the same process. See 8.1.

items.text: Why read Windows Update on a reboot loop?
options: A pending update is a change window
Updates never cause restarts
It is a reason to disable Defender
It means the board has failed
items.correct: A pending update is a change window
items.explanation: A pending or failed update can restart the PC repeatedly, so Update history is evidence for a reboot loop and a reason to plan a change window. Updates do cause restarts, and none of this justifies turning Defender off or blaming the board. See 8.2.

items.text: Which tool shows a day-by-day timeline of crashes alongside software and driver installs?
options: Disk Management (diskmgmt.msc)
Reliability Monitor (perfmon /rel)
Device encryption in Settings
The Windows Update troubleshooter tool
items.correct: Reliability Monitor (perfmon /rel)
items.explanation: Reliability Monitor correlates failures with installs, which helps date a fault to a change.

items.text: Time skew of 10 minutes appears on a domain client; logons intermittently fail. Root cause class?
options: Expired DNS records on the client
An expired computer-account password
A corrupt local user profile
Kerberos clock-skew limits
items.correct: Kerberos clock-skew limits
items.explanation: Kerberos rejects tickets when client and domain controller clocks differ by more than the allowed skew (5 minutes by default).

items.text: Which Windows lab view is the counterpart of About This Mac?
options: Settings → Apps → Installed apps
Settings → Windows Update
Settings → Accounts → Your info
Settings → System → About
items.correct: Settings → System → About
items.explanation: About This Mac shows the model, chip, memory and macOS version, and Settings → System → About shows the same identity facts on Windows. Installed apps, Windows Update and Your info show other things. See 9.2.

items.text: A Mac user asks for access to a share they have never had. How do you classify it?
options: Clean install
Service request / entitlement
Break/fix — the network card
Security incident
items.correct: Service request / entitlement
items.explanation: Access the user has never had is new entitlement, so it is a service request. Nothing is broken, so it is not break/fix or a security incident, and a clean install would change nothing. See 9.3 / 1.1.

items.text: A Linux share holds both Plan.docx and plan.docx. What does a Windows user browsing the share usually see?
options: Both files, listed side by side under their original names and sizes
An error message, because SMB cannot share folders that live on Linux
Two copies of whichever file was saved most recently, under one name
Only one, as Windows treats names case-insensitively by default
items.correct: Only one, as Windows treats names case-insensitively by default
items.explanation: Linux file names are case-sensitive, so two files can differ only by case. Windows treats names case-insensitively by default, so it shows only one of them. The fix is a naming rule on the Linux side, not a Windows repair.

items.text: Windows Event Viewer shows repeated failed logons from many internal IPs against one account. Best immediate action?
options: Unlock the account so the user can work
Ignore it as normal authentication noise
Reboot the domain controller to clear it
Protect the account and investigate per process
items.correct: Protect the account and investigate per process
items.explanation: Many sources against one account suggest an attack. Follow the incident process: protect the account, preserve logs and look for lateral movement.

items.text: Which attack is best mitigated by application allow-listing on fixed-function kiosks?
options: Distributed denial of service
Wi-Fi eavesdropping
Running unauthorised programs such as ransomware
Phishing emails reaching inboxes
items.correct: Running unauthorised programs such as ransomware
items.explanation: Allow-listing runs only approved programs, blocking unauthorised binaries such as ransomware.

items.text: A user typed their password into a phishing page. Which step is part of the follow-up?
options: Ask the user to change their desk phone PIN
Check the mailbox for new forwarding rules
Reinstall the user’s web browser at once
Clear the user’s browser history and cache
items.correct: Check the mailbox for new forwarding rules
items.explanation: Attackers often add forwarding or deletion rules; these are checked along with sessions and MFA methods.

items.text: Which Application-log event usually records a program crash, with the faulting module?
options: Kernel-Power, event ID 41
Service Control Manager, event ID 7036
User Profile Service, ID 1530
Application Error, event ID 1000
items.correct: Application Error, event ID 1000
items.explanation: Application Error 1000 names the faulting application and module; Kernel-Power 41 is an unexpected shutdown.

items.text: Repair vs rebuild: default?
options: Repair or in-place upgrade first
Rebuild from a clean image first
Always reset to factory defaults
Replace the disk, then reinstall
items.correct: Repair or in-place upgrade first
items.explanation: Use the least disruptive fix first: an app repair or in-place upgrade keeps apps and data. A clean image, a factory reset or a new disk are bigger changes for when repair has failed and the user’s data is backed up. See 11.3 / 8.1.

items.text: Windows resource monitor shows a process locking a log file you need to truncate. Best approach?
options: Delete the folder in Safe Mode
Stop the owning service gracefully, then manage the file
Delete the file while the service runs
Take ownership and force-delete it
items.correct: Stop the owning service gracefully, then manage the file
items.explanation: Stop the owning service or process gracefully, then manage the file; forcing it can corrupt data.

items.text: Logon sits on “Applying user settings” for five minutes. Which evidence helps most?
options: The firmware event log and the boot order list
GroupPolicy Operational log and gpresult /h
The printer queue and the spooler status
The Wi-Fi channel and the signal strength
items.correct: GroupPolicy Operational log and gpresult /h
items.explanation: User-policy delays (scripts, drive maps) show in the GroupPolicy Operational log and the gpresult report.

items.text: Adding production DNS after 1500 against policy is:
options: Repair
Optional
Always allowed
A change
items.correct: A change
items.explanation: Adding a production DNS record outside the agreed window and against policy is a change: it needs a request, approval and a backout plan. It is not a repair, and policy says it is not optional or always allowed. See 12.1 / 1.3.

items.text: During repair you see files suggesting a possible crime. What should you do?
options: Open the files to confirm what they are before reporting
Copy the files to a USB stick as evidence
Discuss it with colleagues to get their views
Stop, record the facts and report through the procedure
items.correct: Stop, record the facts and report through the procedure
items.explanation: Do not investigate, copy or discuss; record facts and report through the named channel.

items.text: RAID vs backup vs snapshot?
options: The same — all three protect against site loss
RAID is the off-site copy; snapshots are the local copy
Snapshots are the tenant backup; RAID is off-site
Different — RAID and snapshots are not off-site copies
items.correct: Different — RAID and snapshots are not off-site copies
items.explanation: RAID keeps a volume running through a disk failure, and a snapshot is a point-in-time state on the same system; neither is a separate off-site copy. Only a backup kept elsewhere protects against site loss, deletion or ransomware. See 12.3 / 3.2 / 6.3.

items.text: A laptop is sanitised and recycled. How should its asset record change?
options: Status disposed, with date and sanitisation reference
Delete the record so that the asset list stays short
Keep it marked “in use” until the warranty ends
Move it to the new owner listed on the invoice
items.correct: Status disposed, with date and sanitisation reference
items.explanation: Asset records track a device through disposal; the sanitisation reference is the evidence.

items.text: ipconfig /all belongs in:
options: The ticket as evidence
Only in your own notes
The password field
Nowhere — it changes too often
items.correct: The ticket as evidence
items.explanation: ipconfig /all output is evidence of what the PC thought its network settings were at that time, so paste it into the ticket with the command. Keeping it in private notes or leaving it out loses that record, and it never goes in a password field. See 13.2 / 5.1.

items.text: Firewall during 13.4?
options: Only on Macs
Stays on
Off
Optional
items.correct: Stays on
items.explanation: The firewall stays on during the name-resolution labs, as in every chapter. DNS faults are found with lease, IP and name tests, not by removing protection. See 13.4.

items.text: Before changing the lab VM:
options: Delete host snapshots
Inventory
clean
Disable Defender
items.correct: Inventory
items.explanation: Inventory the lab VM (name, edition, disks, network) before changing anything, so you can tell what changed. Deleting host snapshots, clean and disabling Defender are destructive or unsafe. See 13.1 / 2.6.

items.text: A lease renew fails after a desk move while other ports on the row work. What should you do next?
options: Run netsh int ip reset and then restart the PC
Perform a full Settings network reset now
Try a known-good port and escalate the bad one
Reinstall the network adapter driver first
items.correct: Try a known-good port and escalate the bad one
items.explanation: Evidence points to the switch port or VLAN; changing the PC’s stack would alter the wrong thing.

items.text: Which protocol resolves IPv4 addresses to MAC addresses on a LAN?
options: DHCP
ICMP
ARP
DNS
items.correct: ARP
items.explanation: ARP maps an IPv4 address to a MAC address on the local link.

items.text: What is the broadcast address of 172.16.5.64/27?
items.explanation: A /27 block is 32 addresses: 172.16.5.64–172.16.5.95, so .95 is the broadcast.

items.text: Which scenario correctly prefers UDP over TCP?
options: An interactive SSH session
A file transfer that must arrive intact
Live voice or video, where low delay matters most
Loading a web page over HTTP/1.1
items.correct: Live voice or video, where low delay matters most
items.explanation: Live voice/video values low delay over recovering every packet, which suits UDP.

items.text: 802.1Q tagging is used to?
options: Carry VLAN identity on trunk links
Encrypt frames between switches
Bundle links into one logical link
Prevent loops between switches
items.correct: Carry VLAN identity on trunk links
items.explanation: 802.1Q inserts a VLAN tag so a trunk can carry many VLANs.

items.text: A copper run fails certification at 100m+ for 10GBASE-T. Likely factor?
options: The NIC duplex and speed settings
The VLAN assigned to the access port
The switch’s PoE power budget
The 100 m channel limit and cable category
items.correct: The 100 m channel limit and cable category
items.explanation: Beyond the 100 m channel, and with lower categories or poor installation, 10GBASE-T will not certify.

items.text: Which command-line tool on many systems shows the path packets take?
options: netstat
traceroute/tracert
nslookup
arp -a
items.correct: traceroute/tracert
items.explanation: traceroute (tracert on Windows) lists the router hops.

items.text: A wireless survey shows high channel utilization on 2.4 GHz. Best first design response?
options: Add more APs on channel 6
Move clients to 5/6 GHz and cut channel overlap
Raise every AP’s transmit power to maximum
Use 40 MHz channels on 2.4 GHz
items.correct: Move clients to 5/6 GHz and cut channel overlap
items.explanation: 2.4 GHz has only three non-overlapping channels; move capable clients to 5/6 GHz and reduce co-channel overlap.

items.text: In what order do the DHCP DORA messages occur?
options: Discover, Request, Offer, Acknowledge
Offer, Discover, Acknowledge, Request
Request, Offer, Discover, Acknowledge
Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge
items.correct: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge
items.explanation: The client discovers, servers offer, the client requests one offer and that server acknowledges.

items.text: A zero-trust approach most strongly emphasizes?
options: Verification and least privilege everywhere
Relying on a VPN for access control
Blocking all remote access
Trusting devices inside the perimeter
items.correct: Verification and least privilege everywhere
items.explanation: Zero trust verifies every request and grants least privilege regardless of network location.

items.text: A user VLAN cannot reach the Internet; the server VLAN can. Both use the same core. First isolation step?
options: Reboot the core switch to clear it
Compare routing, ACL and NAT rules per VLAN
Replace the user VLAN’s uplink cable
Disable Spanning Tree on the core
items.correct: Compare routing, ACL and NAT rules per VLAN
items.explanation: Shared core works for one VLAN, so compare what differs per VLAN: routes, ACL/firewall rules and NAT.

items.text: Which status update is most useful to stakeholders?
options: Impact, current action, next update time
Technical details of every command run
“Working on it” every few minutes
A promise of when it will be fixed
items.correct: Impact, current action, next update time
items.explanation: Stakeholders need impact, what is being done and when they will hear next; avoid promises you cannot keep.

items.text: After the incident, what should be updated?
options: Nothing more, as long as the service has been restored
The user’s password
Diagrams, configs and the runbook to match the change
Only the ticket status
items.correct: Diagrams, configs and the runbook to match the change
items.explanation: Documentation that matches reality is what makes the next incident faster.

items.text: Which command shows interface addresses and up/down status in one short list?
options: show running-config
show vlan brief
show version
show ip interface brief
items.correct: show ip interface brief
items.explanation: show ip interface brief lists each interface with its IP address, status and protocol.
